blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
summarise(), from the dplyr package, makes a new data frame. It has one row for each group, or a single row for the whole data frame when there are no groups.

The function n() gives the number of rows in the group, whatever they hold. The function sd() gives the standard deviation, dividing by one less than the count. A quantile is the value below which a given share of the data lies. The function quantile() prints the 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% ones; 0% and 100% are the smallest and largest values. IQR() gives the interquartile range. Both use the seventh of nine rules for placing a quantile between two values, unless told otherwise.

group_by() marks a data frame as grouped by one or more columns, so that the next verbs work group by group. ungroup() removes the marking. The .by argument of summarise() groups for that one step only, and leaves the result ungrouped.

count(a) gives the number of rows for each value of a. write_csv(data, path), from the readr package, writes a data frame to a CSV file.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
The shape of the answer tells you what you asked for. Three species give three rows. If you expected three rows and got eight, you grouped by something else as well.

Put the count beside every summary.

Quartiles have more than one recipe. None is wrong. Say which you used.

Never copy a number off the screen into a report. If the data change, rerun the script and the file changes with them.

A summary describes the rows in your file. It is not, by itself, a figure for anyone outside it.

blocks.alt: A bar chart of three species. Adelie 3701 grams, Gentoo 5076 grams, Chinstrap 3733 grams, on an axis that starts at zero.
blocks.caption: Mean body mass of the penguins in the file, by species, from the summary by species: Adelie 3701 g from 151 body masses, Gentoo 5076 g from 123, Chinstrap 3733 g from 68. The bars start at zero, so their lengths compare the means. The means describe the rows of this file.

blocks.alt: A grouped bar chart of eight species and sex groups, each with two bars. Share within its species: Adelie female 48.0, male 48.0, sex not recorded 3.95; Chinstrap female 50, male 50; Gentoo female 46.8, male 49.2, sex not recorded 4.03. Share of all 344: 21.2, 21.2, 1.74, 9.88, 9.88, 16.9, 17.7, 1.45.
blocks.caption: The same eight counts of penguins by species and sex, turned into percentages two ways. Still grouped by species, sum(n) adds up within each species, so 73 Adelie females print as 48.0%, a share of the 152 Adelie penguins. Grouped with .by for one step only, sum(n) adds up all 344 rows, and the same 73 are 21.2%. The code ran both times; only the second answers “what share of all the penguins?”.

blocks.alt: A bar chart of three interquartile ranges for the same nine heights: Book 0's method 10 cm, R type 7 7 cm, R type 6 10 cm.
blocks.caption: The interquartile range of the nine children’s heights, 121 to 141 cm, by three rules. Book 0’s median of each half gives 136 - 126 = 10 cm; R’s default, type 7, gives 134 - 127 = 7 cm; type 6 gives 10 cm again. The data are the same in every bar: only the rule for placing a quartile between two values differs, so a methods section names the software and the rule.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with the penguin file, and give the species short names as the section on making new columns did. Keep a copy of body mass under a name without spaces.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins <- penguins_raw |>
  mutate(
    species = case_when(
      Species == "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)" ~ "Adelie",
      Species == "Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)" ~ "Chinstrap",
      Species == "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)" ~ "Gentoo"
    ),
    body_mass_g = `Body Mass (g)`
  )

Ask for the mean body mass of all the penguins:

penguins |>
  summarise(mean_g = mean(body_mass_g))
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_g
   <dbl>
1     NA

One row, as promised, and the answer is NA. Two penguins have no body mass, and one missing value makes the whole mean missing. That is R refusing to guess. Tell mean() to leave the missing values out, and ask for the count beside it:

penguins |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    mean_g = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  n_rows mean_g
   <int>  <dbl>
1    344  4202.

Read the two numbers together. n_rows is 344, every row in the file. The mean was worked out from 342 of them, because na.rm = TRUE dropped the two without a body mass. The count beside the mean is wrong by two, and nothing on the screen says so. Count the values the mean used, not the rows:

mass_by_species <- penguins |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_mass = sum(!is.na(body_mass_g)),
    mean_g = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_g = sd(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_g = median(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr_g = IQR(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = species
  )

mass_by_species
# A tibble: 3 × 7
  species   n_rows n_mass mean_g  sd_g median_g iqr_g
  <chr>      <int>  <int>  <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 Adelie       152    151  3701.  459.     3700  650
2 Gentoo       124    123  5076.  504.     5000  800
3 Chinstrap     68     68  3733.  384.     3700  462.

.by = species asked for one row per species, and there are three rows. Each row has its own two counts. Adelie has 152 rows and 151 body masses; Gentoo has 124 rows and 123; Chinstrap has 68 of each. Those are the two missing values, one in each of two species. The tibble prints the means rounded to fit the screen.

Now put the table where a report can use it, without a hand touching a number. In your own project the output/ folder already exists; the first line makes it if it does not, and does nothing if it does.

dir.create(here::here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)

write_csv(
  mass_by_species,
  here::here("output", "mass_by_species.csv")
)

readLines(here::here("output", "mass_by_species.csv"))
[1] "species,n_rows,n_mass,mean_g,sd_g,median_g,iqr_g"
[2] "Adelie,152,151,3700.662251655629,458.5661259101348,3700,650"
[3] "Gentoo,124,123,5076.016260162602,504.11623665709163,5000,800"
[4] "Chinstrap,68,68,3733.0882352941176,384.3350813871914,3700,462.5"

readLines() prints a text file’s lines as they are, to show what was written. The file holds the full numbers, not the rounded ones on the screen. A report that quotes the Adelie mean takes it from this file. If a corrected body mass arrives next month, you rerun the script, the file changes, and the report’s number can be checked against it.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The table describes the 344 rows of this file: penguins measured on three islands in three seasons. It is not a figure for all penguins of these species, and the file’s documentation makes no such claim.

Leaving out missing values is a choice. Here two body masses out of 344 are missing, and the choice barely matters. When a quarter of the values are missing, the mean of the rest may describe a different group of penguins, or patients, from the one you meant. The section on missing values says how to count and report them.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Here is a trap that catches people moving between Book 0 and R. Take nine made-up heights of children, in centimetres, already in order: 121, 125, 127, 128, 132, 133, 134, 138, 141.

Work the quartiles by Book 0’s method first. There are nine values, an odd count, so leave the middle one, 132, out of both halves. The lower half is 121, 125, 127, 128. Its median, the first quartile, is halfway between 125 and 127: 126. The upper half is 133, 134, 138, 141. Its median, the third quartile, is halfway between 134 and 138: 136. The interquartile range is 136 minus 126, which is 10.

first quartile = (125 + 127) divided by 2 = 126
third quartile = (134 + 138) divided by 2 = 136
interquartile range = 136 - 126 = 10

Now ask R:

heights_cm <- c(121, 125, 127, 128, 132, 133, 134, 138, 141)

quantile(heights_cm)
IQR(heights_cm)
  0%  25%  50%  75% 100%
 121  127  132  134  141
[1] 7

R says the first quartile is 127, the third is 134, and the interquartile range is 7. Your hand calculation said 126, 136 and 10. The median, 132, agrees.

Neither of you made a mistake. There is more than one rule for where a quartile sits when it falls between two values. The help page for quantile() lists nine, and R uses type 7 unless told otherwise. The same page says SPSS uses type 6. Ask for type 6:

quantile(heights_cm, type = 6)
  0%  25%  50%  75% 100%
 121  126  132  136  141

Type 6 gives 126 and 136, the same as Book 0’s method on these nine values. That agreement is a property of this set of numbers. It is not a rule that the two methods always agree.

Method First quartile (cm) Third quartile (cm) Interquartile range (cm)
Book 0, median of each half 126 136 10
R, type 7 (the default) 127 134 7
R, type 6 (said to be SPSS’s) 126 136 10

So when a colleague’s SPSS table and your R output disagree on a quartile, check the rule before you check the data. And in your own methods section, name the software and the rule.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The nine heights are made up; they show the arithmetic and describe no children.

With hundreds of values the rules land very close together, because neighbouring values in a big sorted list are close. The disagreement is largest with few values, which is exactly when a thesis table is most likely to be checked by hand.

blocks.label: Illustration 3
blocks.html:
Now group by two columns at once, species and sex, and work out each group’s share of all the penguins. Continue in the same session.

penguins |>
  group_by(species, Sex) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n))
`summarise()` has grouped output by 'species'. You can override using
the `.groups` argument.
# A tibble: 8 × 4
# Groups:   species [3]
  species   Sex        n   pct
  <chr>     <chr>  <int> <dbl>
1 Adelie    FEMALE    73 48.0
2 Adelie    MALE      73 48.0
3 Adelie    <NA>       6  3.95
4 Chinstrap FEMALE    34 50
5 Chinstrap MALE      34 50
6 Gentoo    FEMALE    58 46.8
7 Gentoo    MALE      61 49.2
8 Gentoo    <NA>       5  4.03

Eight rows, not six. Two species have penguins whose sex was not recorded, and NA became a group of its own: 6 Adelie and 5 Gentoo. A summary never hides a missing category. It prints it, and you decide what to say about it.

Read the message too. summarise() removed only the last grouping column, Sex, so the result is still grouped by species. The line # Groups: species [3] says so.

The first row says 48.0% for Adelie females. But 73 is not 48% of 344. Because the result was still grouped by species, sum(n) added up within each species: 73 divided by 152, not by 344. The code ran, gave tidy numbers, and answered a different question.

Group for one step only with .by, and the result comes back ungrouped:

penguins |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = c(species, Sex)) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n))
# A tibble: 8 × 4
  species   Sex        n   pct
  <chr>     <chr>  <int> <dbl>
1 Adelie    MALE      73 21.2
2 Adelie    FEMALE    73 21.2
3 Adelie    <NA>       6  1.74
4 Gentoo    FEMALE    58 16.9
5 Gentoo    MALE      61 17.7
6 Gentoo    <NA>       5  1.45
7 Chinstrap FEMALE    34  9.88
8 Chinstrap MALE      34  9.88

Now 73 Adelie females are 21.2% of all 344. The rows come in the order each group first appears in the file, whereas group_by() sorted them. If you do use group_by(), end the pipe with ungroup() before anything else touches the result.

For counts alone there is a shorter way, met in the section on categories. count(species, Sex) gives the same eight rows and counts, and an ungrouped result.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The percentages describe the rows of this file. Whether 21.2% of all penguins on these islands are female Adelies is a question about how the birds were chosen for study, which no summary can answer.

Grouping and summarising is also what a database query does; the next rung runs the same summaries on a whole survey in a database.

The leftover grouping trap needs two grouping columns. With one column, summarise() removes it and the result comes back ungrouped, so the trap waits until the day you add a second.

points.html: Print the count beside every summary, and print the right count. n() counts rows. With na.rm = TRUE, a mean uses only the rows that have a value, so count those with sum(!is.na(x)).
The error is to think na.rm = TRUE fixes missing values. It only leaves them out, without a word.
Check the shape of the result before reading a number.
After group_by() on two columns, summarise() leaves the result grouped by the first. A percentage worked out next is a percentage within each group, not of the total.
When two tables disagree on a quartile, ask which rule each used before you suspect the data.
A number copied off the screen into a thesis cannot be traced back.
When a trainee shows you a table of means, ask first for the count in each row and for how many values were missing. Then ask for the median beside the mean, as Book 0 taught.

A summary describes the rows in your file. It is not an estimate for any population unless the rows were chosen to stand for one. For a survey, it also needs the survey’s sample weights, which a later book teaches.

blocks.prompt: Add to your penguin script a summary of flipper length by island. Give, for each island, the number of rows, the number of flipper lengths used, the mean and the median in millimetres. Write the table to output/flipper_by_island.csv, and say which island’s mean rests on the fewest measurements.
blocks.answer:
library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

flipper_by_island <- penguins_raw |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_flipper = sum(!is.na(`Flipper Length (mm)`)),
    mean_mm = mean(`Flipper Length (mm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_mm = median(`Flipper Length (mm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = Island
  )

flipper_by_island

dir.create(here::here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(flipper_by_island, here::here("output", "flipper_by_island.csv"))
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  Island    n_rows n_flipper mean_mm median_mm
  <chr>      <int>     <int>   <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Torgersen     52        51    191.       191
2 Biscoe       168       167    210.       214
3 Dream        124       124    193.       193

Three islands, three rows. Torgersen’s mean rests on the fewest flipper lengths: 51 of its 52 rows have one. Biscoe and Torgersen each lost one penguin to a missing flipper length; Dream lost none. The file in output/ holds the full numbers, and rerunning the script rewrites it.

blocks.prompt: A colleague’s thesis table gives “Mean haemoglobin 11.2 g/dL (n = 312)” for the women in her study. She ran mean(hb, na.rm = TRUE) in the console and read the answer off the screen. She typed it into the Word table, with nrow() of her data frame as the n. Say what can be wrong with that number and its n, and how her script should produce them instead.
blocks.answer:
Two things can be wrong, and nobody can now tell whether they are.

The n may not be the n behind the mean. The function nrow() counts every woman in the data frame. na.rm = TRUE left out any woman with no haemoglobin result. If 20 results were missing, the mean came from 292 women and the table says 312.

The number has no trail. It was read off a screen and typed. If a value in the data is later corrected, or a typing slip turned 11.2 into 12.1, nothing connects the table to the code.

Instead, the script should compute the summary with summarise(): n() for the rows, sum(!is.na(hb)) for the results used, and the mean and median. It should write that table to output/ with write_csv(). The thesis table is then copied from that file, which the script rewrites every time it runs. A later book shows documents in which the code writes each number itself.

blocks.prompt: A first-year resident has ten minutes and a whiteboard. She has just made a table of mean BMI by district from a screening register. She does not see why you want a count in every row. Teach her.
blocks.answer:
Draw two made-up rows on the board. District A: mean BMI 24.0 kg/m2. District B: mean BMI 27.0 kg/m2. Ask her which district has the higher BMI. She will say B.

Now add a count to each row: A, 2,400 adults; B, 4 adults. Ask again. The difference is the same three units, but B’s mean is four people. One person of high BMI who happened to come that day could have made it.

Then add a second count: values used. Say B screened 40 adults but only 4 had weight and height recorded. Now the mean describes the 4 who were measured, and nobody knows whether they are like the other 36.

Write the rule under the table. Every summary row carries the number of rows and the number of values used. In R that is n() and sum(!is.na(x)), inside the same summarise() as the mean. Then the counts can never drift away from the number they describe.

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, name three ways a table of summaries by group can be wrong, or misleading, without any error message.
blocks.answer:
Any three of these:

  • The count printed is n(), the rows, while the mean used fewer values because na.rm = TRUE left the missing ones out.
  • A percentage worked out after group_by() on two columns is a share within each group, not of the total, because the result was still grouped.
  • A quartile differs from another tool’s because the two use different rules.
  • A group of NA, such as penguins with no sex recorded, is dropped from the report without a word, though the summary printed it.
  • A number was copied off the screen and later typed wrongly, or not updated when the data changed.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up table:

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

scores <- tibble(score = c(4, 9, 5))

Write one line that gives the number of rows and the mean score, in one row.
blocks.answer:
scores |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_score = mean(score))
# A tibble: 1 × 2
      n mean_score
  <int>      <dbl>
1     3          6

One row: 3 rows, and a mean of 6, since 4 plus 9 plus 5 is 18, and 18 divided by 3 is 6.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up table of two groups:

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

visits <- tibble(
  clinic = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A"),
  patients = c(12, 7, 9, 11, 6)
)

Give the total number of patients for each clinic. Before you run it, say how many rows the answer will have.
blocks.answer:
Two clinics, so two rows.

visits |>
  summarise(total = sum(patients), .by = clinic)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  clinic total
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 A         27
2 B         18

Clinic A: 12 plus 9 plus 6 is 27. Clinic B: 7 plus 11 is 18.

blocks.prompt: Use Book 0’s method, the median of each half, on the four numbers 2, 4, 6 and 8. Work out the first quartile, the third quartile and the interquartile range. Then run quantile() and IQR() on the same four numbers in R. Say why the answers differ.
blocks.answer:
Book 0: the lower half is 2 and 4, so the first quartile is halfway between them, 3. The upper half is 6 and 8, so the third quartile is 7. The interquartile range is 7 minus 3, which is 4.

quantile(c(2, 4, 6, 8))
IQR(c(2, 4, 6, 8))
  0%  25%  50%  75% 100%
 2.0  3.5  5.0  6.5  8.0
[1] 3

R gives 3.5 and 6.5, and an interquartile range of 3. R’s default, type 7, places a quartile by a different rule from Book 0’s. Neither is a mistake. On four values the rules are far apart; on hundreds they land close together.

blocks.prompt:
Read the penguin file.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

For each island, give the number of rows and the number of different species found there. (n_distinct(x) counts the different values in x.)
blocks.answer:
penguins_raw |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_species = n_distinct(Species),
    .by = Island
  )
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  Island    n_rows n_species
  <chr>      <int>     <int>
1 Torgersen     52         1
2 Biscoe       168         2
3 Dream        124         2

Torgersen: 52 rows, 1 species. Biscoe: 168 rows, 2 species. Dream: 124 rows, 2 species. The three counts of rows add up to 344, every row in the file. Only Adelie penguins were sampled on all three islands.

blocks.prompt:
Read the penguin file.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Give the median body mass in grams for each value of Sex, with the number of rows and the number of body masses used. Say what the third row is, and why it is there.
blocks.answer:
penguins_raw |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_mass = sum(!is.na(`Body Mass (g)`)),
    median_g = median(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = Sex

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  Sex    n_rows n_mass median_g
  <chr>   <int>  <int>    <dbl>
1 MALE      168    168     4300
2 FEMALE    165    165     3650
3 <NA>       11      9     4100

Males: 168 rows, median 4300 g. Females: 165 rows, median 3650 g. The third row is NA: 11 penguins whose sex was not recorded, 9 of them with a body mass. A summary does not drop a missing category; it prints it as a group. Say how many penguins had no sex recorded, and do not quietly leave them out of the table.

Read the penguin file.

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Make a table of culmen length by species: the number of values used, the mean and the standard deviation. The culmen is the ridge of the bill, measured in millimetres. Write it to output/culmen_by_species.csv. Then show that the file exists and how many lines it has.
blocks.answer:
culmen_by_species <- penguins_raw |>
  summarise(
    n_culmen = sum(!is.na(`Culmen Length (mm)`)),
    mean_mm = mean(`Culmen Length (mm)`, na.rm = TRUE),

dir.create(here::here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(culmen_by_species, here::here("output", "culmen_by_species.csv"))

file.exists(here::here("output", "culmen_by_species.csv"))

[1] TRUE
[1] 4

The file exists, with 4 lines: a header and one line per species. The function sd() divides by one less than the count, as Book 0 does for a sample. The numbers in the file are the ones a report should quote.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague runs this and writes in her notes: “Adelie and Gentoo body masses were not recorded; only Chinstrap has data.”

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  summarise(mean_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`), .by = Species)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Species                                   mean_g
  <chr>                                      <dbl>
1 Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)          NA
2 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)            NA
3 Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)  3733.

Find what broke.
blocks.answer:
Nothing is wrong with the data. mean() returns NA if even one value in the group is missing, unless told to leave missing values out. Adelie and Gentoo each have one missing body mass; Chinstrap has none. Count, then summarise:

penguins_raw |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(`Body Mass (g)`)),
    mean_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = Species
  )
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  Species                                   n_rows n_missing mean_g
  <chr>                                      <int>     <int>  <dbl>
1 Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)          152         1  3701.
2 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)            124         1  5076.
3 Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)     68         0  3733.

Adelie: 1 missing of 152. Gentoo: 1 missing of 124. Both have a mean.

Why the wrong reading looks reasonable: NA means “not available”, and the note took that to mean the whole column was not available. It meant one value was.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague’s table of Gentoo body mass reads “n = 124, mean 5076 g”. Here is his code.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  filter(Species == "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)") |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 2
      n mean_g
  <int>  <dbl>
1   124  5076.

The mean is right. Find what is wrong with the table.
blocks.answer:
The n counts rows, not body masses. One Gentoo penguin has no body mass, so the mean was worked out from 123 values, not 124.

penguins_raw |>
  filter(Species == "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)") |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_mass = sum(!is.na(`Body Mass (g)`)),
    mean_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  n_rows n_mass mean_g
   <int>  <int>  <dbl>
1    124    123  5076.

The table should read “n = 123” for the mean, and say that 1 of 124 had no body mass.

Why the wrong n looks reasonable: n() is the count every example shows beside a mean. With no missing values it is the right one. The error only appears in a group with a gap.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague wants each species-and-sex group’s share of all the penguins, and reports “Gentoo males are 49.2% of the penguins in the file.”

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  group_by(Species, Sex) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  filter(Sex == "MALE")
`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Species'. You can override using
the `.groups` argument.
# A tibble: 3 × 4
# Groups:   Species [3]
  Species                                   Sex       n   pct
  <chr>                                     <chr> <int> <dbl>
1 Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)       MALE     73  48.0
2 Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica) MALE     34  50
3 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)         MALE     61  49.2

Find what broke.
blocks.answer:
After summarise(), the result is still grouped by Species: the message says so. So sum(n) adds up within each species. 61 Gentoo males are 49.2% of 124 Gentoo penguins, not of all 344.

Count instead, which returns an ungrouped result:

penguins_raw |>
  count(Species, Sex) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  filter(Sex == "MALE")
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  Species                                   Sex       n   pct
  <chr>                                     <chr> <int> <dbl>
1 Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)       MALE     73 21.2
2 Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica) MALE     34  9.88
3 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)         MALE     61 17.7

Gentoo males are 17.7% of the 344 rows in the file. count() returns an ungrouped result, so sum(n) is 344.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: 49.2% is a sensible share for males in one species, so nothing about the number looks off. Only the denominator changed, and the denominator is not printed.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague runs this to get mean body mass by short species name:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
penguins_raw |>
  summarise(
    mean_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = species
  ) |>
  mutate(
    species = case_when(
      species == "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)" ~ "Adelie",
      species == "Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)" ~ "Chinstrap",
      species == "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)" ~ "Gentoo"
    )
  )
Error in `summarise()`:
! Can't subset columns that don't exist.
✖ Column `species` doesn't exist.

Read the error. Say what broke and fix it.
blocks.answer:
The file’s column is Species, with a capital S. R tells capitals from small letters, so .by = species names a column that does not exist yet. The short names have to be made before the summary groups by them:

penguins_raw |>
  mutate(
    species = case_when(
      Species == "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)" ~ "Adelie",
      Species == "Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)" ~ "Chinstrap",
      Species == "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)" ~ "Gentoo"
    )
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mean_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = species
  )
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   mean_g
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 Adelie     3701.
2 Gentoo     5076.
3 Chinstrap  3733.

Three rows, one per short name. A summary keeps only the grouping columns and the summaries, so make every column you will group by before summarise(), not after.

Why the wrong code looks reasonable: the plan, “summarise, then rename”, is fine in words. But after summarise() the long Species column would be the only one left to rename, and its name is not the one the code used.

blocks.prompt: A made-up draft thesis says: “Gentoo penguins (n = 124) were heavier than Adelie penguins (n = 152), with mean body masses of 5076 g and 3701 g.” Check every number in the sentence against the penguin file. Then say what the result does not establish.
blocks.answer:
library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  filter(Species != "Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)") |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_mass = sum(!is.na(`Body Mass (g)`)),
    mean_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_g = median(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = Species
  )
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  Species                             n_rows n_mass mean_g median_g
  <chr>                                <int>  <int>  <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)    152    151  3701.     3700
2 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)      124    123  5076.     5000

The means match, once rounded: 3701 g for Adelie and 5076 g for Gentoo. The counts do not describe the means. Each n is the number of rows; each mean used one value fewer, 151 and 123. The sentence should give those, or say that one body mass was missing in each species. The medians, 3700 g and 5000 g, tell the same story as the means.

What it does not establish:

  • That Gentoo penguins in general are heavier. These are the penguins in one study, on certain islands in certain seasons.
  • How large the difference is against the spread within each species, or whether it could be chance. That needs the standard deviations and a method from the statistics books.
  • Why they differ. Species is not the only thing that differs between the two groups: they were also sampled on different islands.

blocks.prompt: In a made-up lab meeting, someone says: “Male penguins in this dataset average about 4.5 kg.” Turn the sentence into code, run it, and say what the result does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Body mass is in grams, so 4.5 kg is 4500 g. Summarise by sex, with counts:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  summarise(
    n_mass = sum(!is.na(`Body Mass (g)`)),
    mean_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = Sex
  )

penguins_raw |>
  filter(Sex == "MALE") |>
  summarise(
    n_mass = sum(!is.na(`Body Mass (g)`)),
    mean_g = mean(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = Species
  )
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  Sex    n_mass mean_g
  <chr>   <int>  <dbl>
1 MALE      168  4546.
2 FEMALE    165  3862.
3 <NA>        9  4006.
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  Species                                   n_mass mean_g
  <chr>                                      <int>  <dbl>
1 Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)           73  4043.
2 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)             61  5485.
3 Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)     34  3939.

The 168 males average 4546 g, about 4.5 kg, so the sentence matches the file. Now look inside it. Adelie males average 4043 g and Chinstrap males 3939 g; Gentoo males average 5485 g. No species has males that average about 4.5 kg. The pooled mean sits between a group of lighter birds and a group of heavier ones, and it describes almost no actual penguin.

What it does not establish:

  • Anything about a typical male of any species. Grouping by sex alone mixed three species of quite different size.
  • Anything about the 11 penguins with no sex recorded, who are in neither group.
  • Anything about penguins outside this study.
